content.title: About
content.content: Alfredo sauce is a classic Italian creamy sauce made from butter, heavy cream, and grated Parmesan cheese. It has a smooth, buttery flavor with a subtle cheesy note and is most commonly served with pasta, especially fettuccine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sauce is named after the restaurant "Alfredo" in Rome, where chef Alfredo Di Lelio created it in the early 1900s.
The original recipe used only butter, Parmesan, and pasta, without cream.
In the United States the sauce is often enriched with cream, making it richer and silkier.
Alfredo is frequently used as a base for other sauces, adding mushrooms, chicken, or seafood.
Variations may include garlic, nutmeg, or white wine for extra flavor.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Hard Parmesan cheese is rich in calcium, which supports bone and teeth health.

items.title: Contains vitamins A and D
items.content: Butter and cream provide fat‑soluble vitamins that aid vision and immune function.

items.title: Protein content
items.content: Parmesan adds a modest amount of protein, contributing to tissue repair.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Butter and cream make the sauce calorie‑dense; those watching weight should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The dairy components can cause discomfort for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Allergy to milk or cheese (e.g., Parmesan) requires avoiding the sauce entirely.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Alfredo sauce is traditionally tossed with hot pasta until evenly coated. It can also be used in casseroles, pizza, vegetable dishes, or as a topping for chicken breast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat gently over low heat while stirring to prevent separation. Do not freeze, as the texture may become grainy.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanuts, dry roasted and lightly salted, are whole nuts roasted without added oil and finished with a pinch of salt. They have a distinctive nutty flavor, crunchy texture, and a subtle salty note. Peanuts are enjoyed as a snack, and they are added to salads, baked goods, and Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts belong to the legume family, not true nuts.
Dry roasting preserves most nutrients compared with oil‑fried peanuts.
Peanuts are related to soybeans, beans, and peas.
In the United States peanuts are one of the most popular snack foods, while in Russia they are a common ingredient in confectionery.
A small amount of salt enhances flavor while keeping the natural taste of peanuts.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanuts contain about 25 % protein, making them a good source of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: The majority of fat in peanuts is monounsaturated, which supports heart health.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are important for muscle, nerve, and bone function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in peanuts aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Tree‑nut and legume allergy
items.content: Peanuts are one of the most common allergens; reactions can be severe.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Peanuts are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: The added salt may be a concern for people with hypertension; choose unsalted versions if needed.

items.title: Aflatoxins
items.content: Improper storage can lead to aflatoxin formation; buy from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dry‑roasted, lightly salted peanuts are perfect as a standalone snack, tossed into salads, used in Asian dishes such as pad thai, mixed into muesli or yogurt, or incorporated into baked goods. A quick re‑roast in the oven can boost their aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑sodium pepperoni is a traditional Italian‑style sausage made from pork and beef, seasoned with paprika, garlic and spices, but with less salt. It retains the characteristic smoky heat while being more suitable for those watching their sodium intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pepperoni originated in the United States as a variation of salami adapted to American tastes.
The lower‑salt formulation replaces part of the salt with potassium chloride and relies on stronger spices for flavor.
Pepperoni is most commonly used as a pizza topping, but also works well in sandwiches, salads and snack platters.
Traditional pepperoni gets its bright red color from paprika and sometimes artificial dyes; reduced‑sodium versions often use natural colorants.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pepperoni provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports the nervous system and the formation of red blood cells.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The iron in meat helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Lower salt content makes this product more suitable for people with hypertension or cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to pork or beef.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Like most cured sausages, pepperoni contains saturated fats and should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands may contain nitrites or other preservatives that can be a concern for sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice pepperoni thinly and add it to pizza, pasta, salads, sandwiches, or simply pan‑fry it as a snack. To reduce excess fat, blot the cooked slices with a paper towel.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pepperoni in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. Once opened, it is best used within 2–3 weeks. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.
